question: The 'FuelEU Maritime' Regulation sets out, in Article 23(11), that Member States must allocate the revenue generated from the FuelEU penalties to support the deployment and the use of renewable and low-carbon fuels in the maritime sector, as well as the development of low-carbon infrastructure and technology.

It also requires Member States to publish reports every five years in relation to said financial resources to ensure transparency. At the same time, Article 10(3) of the ETS Maritime Directive (Directive 2003/87/EC, as amended) empowers Member States to decide on the end uses for revenue generated from the auctioning of emission allowances, provided they are related to the goals of the energy and climate transition.

It is clear from the legislation in place that it is essential that the funds generated by both frameworks are used in a transparent and effective manner which is strictly linked to the decarbonisation of maritime transport, the purpose of which being to ensure that such funds are not diverted towards budgetary uses unrelated to the sector’s energy transition. 1.
How will the Commission guarantee that the revenue generated will be reinvested in the maritime sector and what supervisory procedures will it put in place?
Does the Commission envisage adopting common guidelines to harmonise the use of this revenue between Member States?
Does the Commission consider it necessary to implement a reporting framework and impose more rigorous monitoring in order to enhance transparency?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.12.2025) Under Regulation 2023/18051, Member States shall endeavour to ensure that the revenues from the FuelEU penalties are used to support the deployment and the use of renewable and low-carbon fuels in the maritime sector.

By 30 June 2030, and then every five years, Member States shall make public a report on the use of revenue generated from the penalties over the five-year period preceding the year of every such report. Since the Regulation started to apply from 2025, the full reporting cycle still needs to be undertaken. No additional measures for monitoring or harmonisation of reporting are planned at this moment.

Directive 2003/87/EC2 obliges Member States to use their Emissions Trading System (ETS) revenues to support climate action and energy transformation, including in the maritime sector. Most Member States are not required to use the revenue to support the sector.

Only those that receive higher volumes of additional allowances due to their high ratio of shipping companies compared to the population, should use the corresponding share of revenue for maritime-related purposes. The Commission monitors compliance with the Directive to ensure revenue is spent on the listed purposes. Member States submit their reports via Reportnet 3, managed by the European Environment Agency3.

An overview of how each Member State used their ETS revenue is included in the Carbon Market4 and Climate Action Progress Reports5. In addition, the recent Sustainable Transport Investment Plan encourages Member States to invest part of the revenues from the EU ETS to decarbonise the maritime and aviation sectors.
